# Project Findings — LLM SQL Generator

A running record of what was found, why it mattered, and how it was fixed, across
the redesign of this project. Organized so it can be read cold later (e.g. before
an interview) without needing to reconstruct the reasoning from scratch.

See also: `docs/decisions/` for the formal ADRs referenced throughout.

---

## 1. The core architectural bet, and why

**ADR 0001**: SQL is generated by a deterministic compiler over a structured
intermediate representation (QuerySpec) that an LLM populates — not by an LLM
writing SQL text directly. This was a considered decision, not a default: a
baseline (single-shot LLM → raw SQL, no scaffolding) was built specifically to
test the claim empirically, not just assert it (see §5).

**ADR 0002**: The original 4-6-call agent pipeline (schema summarizer → intent →
plan → critic → repair → critic again) was consolidated: the "plan" step (row-grain
candidate generation) is a deterministic graph lookup, not an LLM call; the critic
only runs when static validation actually flags something; schema indexing is
cached per table-shape instead of recomputed every request. Estimated ~69% cost
reduction and 4x fewer sequential LLM round-trips in the common case.

**ADR 0003**: `repair_agent` originally made a second LLM call to reconstruct the
entire QuerySpec from scratch after a critic flagged an issue. This was replaced
with deterministic patch application (`{**before, **patch}`) — found *because* the
LLM-reconstruction approach silently dropped fields it wasn't asked to change,
three separate times, in three different disguises (see §3).

---

## 2. Bugs found through static testing (Phase 0)

These were found by deliberately exercising the deterministic compiler with
realistic inputs, before any live LLM testing began.

| Bug | Impact | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Nested-array alias resolution (`expr_for_path` in `sql_compiler.py`) | Any 2+ level nested array question (the project's headline feature) compiled to SQL referencing the wrong `LATERAL FLATTEN` alias — invalid Snowflake SQL | Compare against original path each iteration, not a mutated copy |
| Filter operators `gt/gte/lt/lte/in` silently dropped | Prompt told the LLM these ops exist; compiler only implemented `eq/neq/contains`. Filters using them vanished from WHERE with no warning | Implemented all ops; unrecognized ops now flagged as issues instead of silently dropped |
| `order_by` requested from LLM, never compiled | "Top N" questions couldn't work regardless of how well the LLM understood the question | Wired into compiler; also fixed `LIMIT` only applying when no `GROUP BY` present |
| Streamlit `c.name`/`c.score` on plain dicts | `AttributeError` the moment a user picked a candidate in the UI | `.get()` access |

---

## 3. Bugs found only through live testing — static tests were not sufficient

This is the single most important methodological finding of the project: **a
fully green test suite (39/39 passing) did not catch any of the bugs in this
section.** Every one was found by actually running the real graph, with a real
LLM, and reading the output by hand. This became a standing rule for the rest of
the project: green tests are necessary but not sufficient; nothing is "done"
without a live run reviewed by eyes.

### 3.1 — False hallucination alarm (a research error, not a code bug)
A golden question (`ecom-13`, "shipping carrier") was built on the assumption no
shipping field existed in the schema. A live run "hallucinated"
`transaction:shipping:method` — except that field was real; the original schema
inspection had only spot-checked `items`/`total_amount`, never dumped the full key
list. **Lesson**: verify against the *complete* field catalog before writing an
adversarial test, not a partial manual read.

Correcting this surfaced a real, more interesting finding underneath the mistake:
the LLM had selected a real-but-wrong field (`shipping:method`, value `"express"`)
instead of the actually-correct one (`shipping:tracking:carrier`, value
`"FedEx"`), and aliased it `shipping_carrier` — a plausible-looking wrong answer
built from a legitimate path. Structural path validation *cannot* catch this class
of error, because nothing about it is structurally wrong. This exact pattern
recurred independently later (§6) on a different schema, confirming it's systemic.

### 3.2 — Invalid `GROUP BY` shape, three-round saga
- **Round 1 (found live)**: `MAX(price) ... SELECT price, name, MAX(price)` — a raw
  column selected alongside an aggregate, absent from `GROUP BY`. Real SQL
  compile error against a real warehouse.
- **Round 2 (bad fix)**: the fix chosen was "drop the ungrouped column from
  SELECT" — which silently deleted user-requested fields (`actor_login` vanished
  from a "which actor has the most events" query). Worse than the original bug:
  fails silently instead of loudly.
- **Round 3 (bad fix again)**: the fix became "add the ungrouped column to
  `GROUP BY`" — which shattered aggregation grain when the added column was
  high-cardinality (e.g. adding a row-unique `event_id` to `GROUP BY` makes every
  `COUNT` trivially 1).
- **Root cause, finally**: the compiler should never *invent* grouping dimensions
  from stray SELECT columns in either direction. `query_spec["group_by"]` is the
  single source of truth; anything selected that's neither aggregated nor in the
  declared `group_by` is a QuerySpec inconsistency — flagged, penalized, sent to
  the critic. Fixed at the actual source: the intent agent shouldn't be adding
  stray raw columns next to aggregations in the first place.

**Lesson**: three rounds of "fix the symptom shown" before anyone asked "why does
this keep happening in new forms." The fourth round stopped and root-caused
instead of patching again.

### 3.3 — Self-referential aggregation
`MAX(price) ... GROUP BY (item_name, price)` — grouping by the exact field being
aggregated, which is a no-op (within any group, a field you grouped by is
constant). Root cause: the intent agent reached for `MAX`+`GROUP BY` on a plain
"what's the single most expensive item" question that needed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`
instead — no aggregation or grouping required at all. Fixed with an explicit
prompt heuristic (top-N-no-qualifier → sort+limit; "per category" → aggregate) plus
a deterministic safety-net check for the self-referential pattern specifically.

### 3.4 — Repair loop silently dropping fields (root cause of §3.2's later rounds)
Traced via a from-scratch repro, not guessed: `repair_agent_node` made its own
LLM call to reconstruct the *entire* QuerySpec, then did a full dict replace of
`state["query_spec"]` — not a merge. Any field the critic's patch didn't
explicitly mention (e.g. `order_by`, `limit`) was silently lost, because the
repair LLM's freshly-generated spec didn't reliably reproduce fields it wasn't
asked to touch. This is the actual mechanism behind repeated "fix drops an
unrelated field" incidents. **Fixed architecturally, not patched**: removed the
second LLM call entirely, replaced with deterministic `{**before, **patch}`
merging of the critic's own structured patch — which also removes an LLM call
from the worst-case pipeline (ties directly into ADR 0002's cost thesis).

### 3.5 — Under-sampling in schema inference
`max_array_samples` defaulted to 3 — schema inference only ever looked at an
array's first 3 elements, regardless of how much real data was actually provided.
Found via a real GitHub dataset where a field (`org`) present on 10/90 events was
invisible to the schema catalog simply because none of the first 3 events had it.
Raised default to 200; this is a systematic fix (any field, any array), not
specific to `org`.

---

## 4. Process / methodology findings (not code bugs, but load-bearing)

- **No version control for most of this session.** Discovered mid-investigation
  while chasing what looked like a fixture mutation (turned out to be investigator
  error, §3.1 — but the absence of `git` to check made that harder to rule out
  than it should have been). Repo connected to its real remote and committed
  properly after this was noticed.
- **A "temporary diagnostic" test accidentally became a permanent, slow, live-LLM
  test in the suite** (15s of a 15.89s total run, real API key required, non-
  deterministic). Deleted; replaced with a rule going forward — `pytest.ini` now
  registers a `@pytest.mark.live` marker and excludes it from default runs.
- **Golden-set ground truth needs independent verification**, not just "this
  is the shape I intended." Every non-adversarial golden question's expected
  answer was computed directly from real data (Python scripts run against the
  actual JSON), not asserted from memory — this is what caught the `ecom-13`
  correction and made the correction trustworthy once found.

---

## 5. Baseline comparison — architecture, not just accuracy

Two baselines, deliberately architecturally isolated from the main pipeline
(`baseline/`, no imports from `workflow.graph`/`workflow.nodes`):

- **Baseline A**: single LLM call, raw JSON sample in the prompt, asked directly
  for Snowflake SQL. No schema index, no structured IR, no validation, no retry.
- **Baseline B**: Baseline A + one unconditional self-critique LLM call (review
  its own SQL, revise or confirm). Deliberately the "obvious naive fix" a naive
  engineer would reach for, without building a validation layer — a fair
  comparison point, not a strawman.

Both reuse the same model (`gpt-4o-mini`) as the real pipeline for a fair
cost/capability comparison.

---

## 6. Degradation study — sample completeness, and the best finding of the project

**Why this study exists**: the product's own UI copy says "paste a representative
sample" with a *one-record* placeholder example, and the repo's own default demo
sample is 2 records. But the golden datasets built for verification purposes were
90 and 200 records — nothing like what a real user would actually provide. The
study runs all three systems (baseline A, baseline B, pipeline) against the same
questions at sample-size tiers [2, 5, 20, full], on data prefixes (not curated
subsamples — deliberately mimics "user pasted whatever was on screen").

### The headline finding
At small tiers, a real sparse field (`org`, present on 10/90 real GitHub events)
is legitimately invisible — expected, correct behavior of sample-based inference.
The interesting part is what each system did about it:

- **Both baselines fabricated a replacement.** Asked "which organization is
  associated with each event," with `org` invisible at tier 2/5, both baselines
  wrote `SPLIT_PART(repo:name, '/', 1) AS organization` — parsing the repo owner
  out of a *different, real* field and presenting it, mislabeled, as the answer
  to a question about a field they'd never seen. Confident, computed, and wrong.
- **The pipeline made a smaller version of the same mistake** — selected
  `repo:name` and aliased it `organization_name`, no fabricated string parsing,
  but still presenting an adjacent real field as though it answers a question it
  doesn't. Static validation had nothing to flag, because nothing is *structurally*
  wrong with the SQL.
- **At tier 20/full, all three systems correctly find and use the real field.**
  Confirms this is a genuine completeness effect, not a permanent flaw.

**Why this matters more than a clean "pipeline wins" result would have**: it
confirms the *exact same failure category* found independently in §3.1
(`ecom-13`'s `shipping:method` vs `shipping:tracking:carrier`) — real path, wrong
concept, no structural signal to catch it — now observed twice, on two different
schemas, in two different systems. That's evidence of a systemic architectural
boundary (deterministic validation catches structural mistakes; it has no
mechanism at all for semantically-wrong-but-syntactically-valid SQL), not a
one-off. The honest framing — "here's a real limitation we found and can name
precisely, twice, independently" — is stronger interview material than an
unqualified win, because it's specific, evidenced, and shows the boundary of what
was actually tested rather than what was assumed.

**A known, stated limitation of the automated detector**: the harness's
`overconfidence_flag` check (built to catch "SQL references a field absent from
this tier's schema") structurally cannot catch the `SPLIT_PART` fabrication,
because every field it touches (`repo:name`) is completely real. Catching "used a
real field to answer a different concept" reliably needs semantic judgment (an
LLM-as-judge), which was deliberately scoped out rather than chased — documented
here as a real, named boundary of the study's automated tooling, not silently
glossed over. This finding was only caught by a manual read of raw SQL after the
automated flag came back `False`.

### A secondary, reassuring finding
`ga4-03` at the *full* tier — real, complete, previously-verified-clean data —
still occasionally reproduced the stray-column `GROUP BY` bug from §3.2, live,
non-deterministically. This time, `static_validate` caught it correctly (score
dropped to 65, issue named specifically, critic engaged). Confirms the safety net
is doing real live work against genuine LLM nondeterminism, not just passing
tests written to match its own behavior.

---

## 7. Numbers worth having ready

- **Estimated cost reduction from ADR 0002**: ~69% best case (1 LLM call vs 4),
  ~$114/mo → ~$35/mo at 100K queries/mo (gpt-4o-mini rates, estimated token counts
  — labeled as estimates, not measured, in the ADR itself).
- **Test suite**: 42 tests, all fake-LLM/deterministic, ~0.8s total runtime.
- **Golden set**: 39 hand-verified questions across 3 real schemas (e-commerce,
  real GitHub Events API data, real GA4 BigQuery public sample data), including
  deliberately adversarial, ambiguous, and known-limitation cases.
- **Distinct real bugs found via live testing that 100% of static tests missed**:
  6 (see §3), each with a permanent regression test added after the fact.

---

## 8. Full-scale comparison study — an honest result, not a clean win

Once the golden set, both baselines, and the eval harness were all individually
verified (§6), a full run across all 39 golden questions produced a result worth
reporting exactly as it landed, not smoothed over: on the (approximate) leaf-token
structural score, **baseline B (self-critique retry) scored 0.971, essentially
tied with or ahead of the pipeline (0.954), with baseline A close behind at 0.937.**

Reading past the aggregate, three real, confirmed-by-reading-the-actual-SQL findings:

- **`ecom-13`** (the shipping-carrier semantic-grounding question, §3.1): both
  baselines correctly selected `shipping:tracking:carrier`; the pipeline selected
  `shipping:method` — the same trap, but this time the freehand baselines got it
  right and the structured pipeline didn't. Plausible reason: raw JSON in a
  baseline's prompt preserves nesting/proximity context (`carrier` sitting right
  next to `tracking`) that a summarized schema catalog can lose.
- **`ecom-12`**: the pipeline generated `user:profile:city` (skipping a real
  `location` level in the path) — `static_validate` correctly flagged it as an
  unknown path, but the comparison harness's approximate token-score metric
  missed it entirely, since the leaf word `city` still matched regardless of the
  wrong parent path. A concrete, confirmed example of the metric's documented
  blind spot, not just a theoretical caveat.
- **`ecom-09`** — the most serious of the three, see §10.

**What this means, honestly**: the pipeline's real advantage isn't "always more
correct on every single question" — on this run, it wasn't. Its advantage is
*knowing when it's wrong* (`static_validate`, tested independently, with
permanent regression coverage) and *fixing the same mistake once instead of
forever* (§2, §3). A baseline that happens to score well today has no such
property and no way to earn one without becoming this architecture. This
reframing is stronger, not weaker, for being honest about a result that didn't
go cleanly one direction — see the retry-exhaustion bug below for what a
close reading of "why" actually turned up.

## 9. Retry-exhaustion silently reporting as success (the most serious bug found via the comparison study)

On `ecom-09` ("purchase or product_view" filter), the critic correctly diagnosed
a real bug **twice** — `"Filter op 'in' requires a list value, got str"` — but its
own repair patch reproduced the identical bug: `"value": "['purchase', 'product_view']"`,
a *string* containing Python list-literal syntax, not an actual JSON array.
Retries exhausted at `max_retries=2`. The compiler correctly (by existing design)
dropped the still-invalid filter — but the **final reported state showed
`static_validate_score: 100`, `issues: []`**, indistinguishable from a candidate
that validated clean on the first pass. The user had no way to know their filter
was silently dropped after two failed repair attempts, and the resulting query
returned every event, unfiltered, not the subset actually asked for.

This is a sharper version of the same pattern as §3.2/§3.4: a mechanism that's
supposed to be the safety net produced a confidently-clean, silently-wrong
result. **Fixed at two points**: `apply_repair_patch` (ADR 0003) now coerces or
rejects malformed patch values instead of blindly merging them (an `in` filter
value that arrives as a Python-repr string is coerced back to a real list, or
the patch is rejected and the prior value kept — never silently accepted
malformed); and the workflow result now carries an explicit
`retry_exhausted_unresolved` flag when retries ran out without reaching a
genuinely clean state, so "gave up, best effort" is never indistinguishable
from "validated clean on the first pass."

## 10. The overconfidence detector's false positive generalized further than first fixed

The degradation study's `overconfidence_flag` check (§6) was first fixed to
exclude root-array keys referenced inside a `LATERAL FLATTEN(input => ...)`
clause (a structural reference, not a data field). A full-scale run surfaced the
same root cause recurring in a different SQL shape: `WHERE f.value:org IS NOT NULL`
— a legitimate, correct defensive null-check on a nested *object* key — flagged
`org` as an unsupported field even when `org:login` was genuinely present in the
schema, because `org` itself (the container) is never a leaf in
`schema_index["fields"]`. The original fix only excluded FLATTEN-input
fragments specifically; the general fix excludes **any** reference to a known
non-leaf container/object key, from any SQL construct, subsuming the earlier
narrower fix rather than sitting alongside it.

## 11. Multi-turn conversational correction — closing a real capability gap, not just a feature add

While researching Snowflake's own Cortex Analyst for the cost benchmark (§13),
its documented feature set included "multi-turn conversations." This project
didn't have an equivalent — so this wasn't picked as a generic nice-to-have, it
directly closes a named gap against the thing being benchmarked.

**Design**: reuses ADR 0003's patch-application machinery rather than building
something new. A chat correction is architecturally the critic's repair loop
with a human supplying the correction instead of an automated critic: one small
LLM call (`interpret_correction`) turns free text ("that's the wrong field, I
want the tracking carrier, not the shipping method") into the *same*
`query_spec_patch` shape the critic already produces, `apply_repair_patch`
merges it deterministically, the result is recompiled and **always**
re-validated (this costs nothing — `static_validate` makes no LLM call — so
there was no real cost/consistency tradeoff to make here; skipping validation
for chat turns specifically would have been an unjustifiable special case).
The existing ADR 0002 critic-skip rule applies unchanged: escalate to the LLM
critic only if the re-validated score is still below threshold.

**Live-verified**, not just unit-tested: run against `ecom-13`'s known real bug
(§3.1/§9 — `shipping:method` selected instead of `shipping:tracking:carrier`).
Turn 1 reproduced the known mistake exactly. The correction turn's patch
correctly targeted `shipping:tracking:carrier`. Turn 2's re-validated SQL
correctly selected the right field, with a real (not skipped) validation score.
One conversation, one real bug, corrected through the same deterministic
machinery the automated critic uses — a concrete demonstration, not a claim.

## 12. Cost benchmarked against Snowflake's own native equivalent

See `docs/decisions/0004-cost-benchmark-vs-snowflake-cortex-analyst.md` for the
full sourcing and caveats. Headline: Snowflake's own Cortex Analyst (native
managed text-to-SQL, GA since 2024) billed **$0.134–$0.40 per query** as of
August 2025 (message-based pricing, edition-dependent credit rates), covering
generation only — the same scope as this project's own estimated
**$0.00035–$0.0014 per query**. Roughly **100–570x cheaper**, same scope on
both sides, sourced from Snowflake's own published pricing model at the time.
Required caveat, every time this is cited: this is a generation-cost comparison,
not a capability-parity claim — Cortex Analyst is a fully managed product with
semantic-model tooling and enterprise support this project doesn't attempt to
replicate. The pricing reference is deliberately anchored to August 2025 (this
project's build window); Snowflake overhauled AI pricing in April 2026.


- Build the live-sanity-check discipline in *before* writing the first line of
  the redesigned pipeline, not after the first round of "tests pass, ship it"
  turned out to be wrong.
- Connect version control before making any changes, not partway through.
- When writing adversarial/known-absent test cases, dump the *complete* field
  catalog programmatically before asserting a field doesn't exist — a partial
  manual read is not verification.

## 13. If asked "what would you do differently"

- Build the live-sanity-check discipline in *before* writing the first line of
  the redesigned pipeline, not after the first round of "tests pass, ship it"
  turned out to be wrong.
- Connect version control before making any changes, not partway through.
- When writing adversarial/known-absent test cases, dump the *complete* field
  catalog programmatically before asserting a field doesn't exist — a partial
  manual read is not verification.
- When a fix's retry loop exhausts without success, that needs to change the
  final report, not disappear into it — "gave up" and "succeeded" must never
  look identical (see §9).
